cues.text: Welcome to Study Session 01 of MIT 8101, Introduction to Information Technology Management.
This course is delivered by Miva Open University, and this lesson is part of the Semester 1 examination preparation material, dated the twenty-fourth of November, 2026.
Before we begin, let me explain how this lesson is designed to work.
It is a continuous, tutor-led lesson, and it is meant to be taken in one sitting.
Plan for roughly two to three hours, and that time includes moments for reflection, so do not rush those pauses.
Please start at the very beginning and work forward in order.
You do not need any prior knowledge.
We assume nothing, and we will build each idea from the ground up.
A few notes about the material you will meet.
The examples and calculations in this lesson are illustrative, which means they are there to help you understand the ideas, unless they are specifically identified as course-material cases.
When a case comes from the course material itself, it will be labelled as such.
This guide is self-contained.
It covers the complete learning scope of Session 01, including enterprise information technology, and the practical lab.
Finally, a caution about examinations.
The suggested examination answers you will find in this guide are not an official marking scheme.
Treat them as helpful models of how an answer might be structured, not as the exact answers your examiners will expect.
With that understood, let us begin the lesson.
Welcome.
In this first section, we'll set out what you are learning and why it matters.
By the end, you should be able to explain IT management and its principles, and describe how technology changes organisational structures.
You should be able to trace the evolution of enterprise IT, analyse African and global applications of it, and recommend improvements to an organisation.
You should also understand the project-management methodologies presented in the textbook.
To see why this matters, imagine a university that buys servers and launches a student portal.
Registration still takes days.
The portal fails during peak demand.
Staff keep paper records, and nobody knows who owns incident resolution.
The university has technology, but it has not managed technology effectively.
Let us define our terms.
Information technology, or IT, includes computing devices, networks, applications, databases, and the people and processes that operate them.
IT management is the deliberate coordination of these resources to achieve organisational objectives reliably, securely and efficiently.
It includes choosing what to build, assigning ownership, funding it, supporting users, managing risks, and evaluating results.
Now consider the difference between technical work and management.
Technical work asks whether the application works.

Management asks that too, but it also asks whether the application solves the right problem, whether people actually use it, whether the organisation can sustain it, and whether the benefits justify the costs.
For example, a working payment API, that is, an application programming interface, which nobody can afford to integrate may be technically successful but commercially unsuccessful.
Finally, notice how the role of IT has changed.
Historically, IT often supported payroll and recordkeeping.
Today it can determine the product itself, how customers access it, and how the organisation competes.
A bank's mobile channel is not merely an administrative convenience; it can be the primary way customers transact.
A recommendation engine can differentiate a streaming business.
This is the distinction between IT as back-office support and IT as a strategic enabler.
